section.title: Holiness in Conduct
section.sectionRationale: This is the heart of the Holiness Code, moving from the sexual ethics of chapter 18 to a comprehensive vision of practical holiness touching worship, family, generosity, honesty, and love of neighbor, all grounded in the command to be holy because the LORD their God is holy.
section.thesis: God calls Israel to imitate His holiness in the whole fabric of ordinary life, worship, family, business, justice, and neighbor love, summarized in the command to love your neighbor as yourself, which Jesus later names as the second great commandment.
section.frameNote: Six movements: the call to holiness rooted in God's own character; laws of worship and family respect; provision for the poor through gleaning; laws of honesty, justice, and love among neighbors; prohibitions against occult and pagan customs; and closing laws of fairness to foreigners, the elderly, and in business.

units.label: Be holy, for I am holy

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“Speak to the whole congregation of Israel and tell them: Be {{qadosh|holy}} because I, the LORD your God, am holy.
Each of you must respect his mother and father, and you must keep My Sabbaths. I am the LORD your God.
Do not turn to idols or make for yourselves molten gods. I am the LORD your God.
When you sacrifice a peace offering to the LORD, you shall offer it for your acceptance.
It shall be eaten on the day you sacrifice it, or on the next day; but what remains on the third day must be burned up.
If any of it is eaten on the third day, it is tainted and will not be accepted.
Whoever eats it will bear his iniquity, for he has profaned what is holy to the LORD. That person must be cut off from his people.

units.label: Gleaning for the poor and the foreigner

verses.text: When you reap the harvest of your land, you are not to reap to the very {{peah|edges}} of your field or gather the gleanings of your harvest.
You must not strip your vineyard bare or gather its fallen grapes. Leave them for the poor and the foreigner. I am the LORD your God.

units.label: Honesty, justice, and love of neighbor
units.note: the great commandment, in seed form

media.alt: Two figures facing each other in a field
media.caption: Love your neighbor as yourself, the command Jesus names as second only to loving God.

verses.text: You must not steal. You must not lie or deceive one another.
You must not swear falsely by My name and so profane the name of your God. I am the LORD.
You must not defraud your neighbor or rob him. You must not withhold until morning the wages due a hired hand.
You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God. I am the LORD.
You must not pervert justice; you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly.
You must not go about spreading slander among your people. You must not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am the LORD.
You must not harbor hatred against your brother in your heart. Directly rebuke your neighbor, so that you will not incur guilt on account of him.
Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but {{ahav|love}} your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD.

You are to keep My statutes. You shall not crossbreed two different kinds of livestock; you shall not sow your fields with two kinds of seed; and you shall not wear clothing made of two kinds of material.

If a man lies carnally with a slave girl promised to another man but who has not been redeemed or given her freedom, there must be due punishment. But they are not to be put to death, because she had not been freed.
The man, however, must bring a ram to the entrance to the Tent of Meeting as his guilt offering to the LORD.
The priest shall make atonement on his behalf before the LORD with the ram of the guilt offering for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven the sin he has committed.
When you enter the land and plant any kind of tree for food, you shall regard the fruit as forbidden. For three years it will be forbidden to you and must not be eaten.
In the fourth year all its fruit must be consecrated as a praise offering to the LORD.
But in the fifth year you may eat its fruit; thus your harvest will be increased. I am the LORD your God.

units.label: No occult practices, no pagan customs

verses.text: You must not eat anything with blood still in it. You must not practice divination or sorcery.
You must not cut off the hair at the sides of your head or clip off the edges of your beard.
You must not make any cuts in your bodies for the dead or put tattoo marks on yourselves. I am the LORD.
You must not defile your daughter by making her a prostitute, or the land will be prostituted and filled with depravity.
You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD.
You must not turn to mediums or spiritists; do not seek them out, or you will be defiled by them. I am the LORD your God.

units.label: Fairness to the elderly, the foreigner, and in business

verses.text: You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God. I am the LORD.
When a foreigner resides with you in your land, you must not oppress him.
You must treat the {{ger|foreigner}} living among you as native-born and love him as yourself, for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt. I am the LORD your God.
You must not use dishonest measures of length, weight, or volume.
You shall maintain honest scales and weights, an honest ephah, and an honest hin. I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.
You must keep all My statutes and all My ordinances and follow them. I am the LORD.”

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart. The chapter's opening command grounds every following law in God's own character: Israel is to be holy not by achieving abstract purity but by conforming its ordinary conduct to the character of the LORD.

peah.gloss: Edge or corner, here of a harvested field. Later Jewish law developed detailed rules for how much of a field's edge to leave unharvested; the principle itself builds generosity toward the poor directly into the structure of ordinary farming.

ahav.gloss: To love. Verse 18's command to love your neighbor as yourself summarizes the whole preceding list of ethical commands and is later named by Jesus as the second great commandment, on which hangs all the Law and the Prophets, Matthew 22:39-40.

ger.gloss: Foreigner, sojourner, resident alien. Verse 34 extends the command to love one's neighbor explicitly to this outsider, grounding it in Israel's own history: you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

basic.context: This chapter gives a sweeping catalog of practical holiness, touching worship, family respect, generosity to the poor, honesty, justice, fair business, and love of neighbor, all repeatedly anchored by the refrain, I am the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter mixes enduring moral commands with old covenant ceremonial and civil markers specific to Israel. Love of neighbor, honesty, and care for the poor and vulnerable are reaffirmed throughout the New Testament as binding on all people; certain boundary markers, like mixed fabric or particular hairstyles, belonged to Israel's distinct identity and are not repeated as commands for the church.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with qadosh, holy, grounding every command in God's own character. Its ethical center is ahav, love, in verse 18's command to love your neighbor as yourself, which verse 34 extends explicitly to the ger, the resident foreigner, on the grounds that Israel itself had once been foreigners in Egypt.
basic.typology: The gleaning law is fulfilled literally when Ruth the Moabite gleans in Boaz's field under this very statute, becoming an ancestress of David and ultimately of Christ. The command to love your neighbor as yourself is named by Jesus as the second great commandment and is perfectly embodied in His own self-giving love.
basic.christ: Jesus cites Leviticus 19:18 directly as the second great commandment, on which hang all the Law and the Prophets, Matthew 22:37-40, and He is the one who fulfills it perfectly, loving His neighbor, even His enemies, to the point of laying down His own life, John 15:13.
basic.god: God's holiness here is not abstract ritual purity but concrete ethical practice woven through worship, family, business, and justice. He identifies with the poor, the deaf, the blind, and the foreigner, and grounds nearly every command in His own character: I am the LORD.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 22:37-40 names Leviticus 19:18 the second great commandment. 1 Peter 1:15-16 applies Be holy, for I am holy directly to the church. Romans 13:8-10 says love fulfills the whole law. Ruth 2:2-3 shows the gleaning law in action, providentially placing Ruth in the line leading to Christ.
basic.oneStory: God's people are called, in the smallest details of daily life, to reflect His own holy character; that call reaches its fulfillment in Christ, who is Himself perfectly holy and perfectly loving, and who unites believers to Himself so that, by His Spirit, they can at last begin to live what this chapter commands.

context.literary:
Leviticus 19 is addressed to 'the whole congregation of Israel,' verse 2, a wider audience than most of the book, and it opens with the sentence that sums up the entire Holiness Code: 'Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy.' Everything that follows unpacks that single line.

The chapter can look like a miscellany, but it has a clear rhythm. After verse 2, the refrain 'I am the LORD' or 'I am the LORD your God' closes a unit fifteen times, verses 3, 4, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 25, 28, 30, 31, 32, 34, 36 and 37. Each command is stamped with the name of the one who gives it.

Many readers have noticed that the Ten Commandments echo throughout the chapter. Parents and Sabbath come first, verse 3, then idols, verse 4. Stealing and lying appear in verse 11, swearing falsely by God's name in verse 12, endangering a neighbour's life in verse 16, and sexual wrong in verse 20. The chapter reads like the Decalogue applied to the field, the marketplace, the courtroom and the heart.

The centre of gravity is verses 11 to 18, four small groups of laws about the neighbour that climb from outward acts to inward attitudes. They begin with theft and fraud, move through the treatment of the disabled and the conduct of courts, and end with hatred in the heart, revenge and grudges, before the summary, 'love your neighbor as yourself,' verse 18. Verse 34 then repeats the same command for the foreigner, so that the second half of the chapter mirrors the first. The chapter ends as it began, with a call to keep all God's statutes, verse 37.
context.historical:
The laws assume a settled farming life that Israel had not yet begun. Harvesting fields, verse 9, tending vineyards, verse 10, and planting fruit trees, verse 23, all look ahead to the land. The gleaning law left the edges of fields unreaped and fallen grapes ungathered, so that the landless could feed themselves by their own work. Deuteronomy 24:19-21 extends it to forgotten sheaves and olives, and the book of Ruth shows it working: a Moabite widow gleans in the field of Boaz, who tells his workers to leave extra stalks for her, Ruth 2:15-16.

Daily wage labour was common, and a day labourer often lived on what he earned that day. Hence the command not to hold back wages until morning, verse 13, which Deuteronomy 24:15 explains, 'because he is poor and depends on them.' Honest measures mattered in a world without standard coinage, where grain was measured by the ephah and oil or wine by the hin, verse 36. The BSB footnotes give the ephah as about twenty-two litres and the hin as about three and two thirds.

Several laws target religious practices of the surrounding peoples. Cutting the body for the dead, verse 28, was a mourning rite; the prophets of Baal cut themselves 'as was their custom,' 1 Kings 18:28. Divination, sorcery and mediums, verses 26 and 31, were ways of seeking hidden knowledge apart from God, and Saul's visit to the medium at Endor, 1 Samuel 28:7, shows how tempting they remained.

Verse 20 deals with a slave woman promised to another man. Because she was not free, the case was not treated as adultery with its death penalty, but the man still had to bring a guilt offering. The law works within a social world very different from ours while restraining its abuses.
context.canonical:
The call 'Be holy, because I am holy' first appears in Leviticus 11:44, attached to food laws, and it echoes through the Holiness Code, Leviticus 20:26. Peter quotes it to scattered believers, 1 Peter 1:16, and Jesus' 'Be perfect, therefore, as your heavenly Father is perfect,' Matthew 5:48, and 'Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful,' Luke 6:36, follow the same pattern of imitating God.

The social laws are taken up by the prophets. Amos 8:5 condemns those who 'reduce the ephah and increase the shekel,' and Micah 6:11 asks whether God can excuse dishonest scales. Jeremiah 22:13 pronounces woe on the king who 'fails to pay their wages,' and Malachi 3:5 promises judgment on those who defraud labourers and deny justice to the foreigner. Ezekiel 22:7 indicts Jerusalem for treating father and mother with contempt and exploiting the foreigner, the concerns of verses 3 and 33. Deuteronomy 10:18-19 roots the love of the foreigner in God's own love, 'He loves the foreigner.'

No verse of Leviticus is quoted more often in the New Testament than verse 18. The BSB footnote lists Matthew 5:43, 19:19 and 22:39, Mark 12:31, Luke 10:27, Romans 13:9, Galatians 5:14 and James 2:8. Jesus pairs it with Deuteronomy 6:5 as the two commands on which all the Law and the Prophets hang. The scribe of Mark 12:33 adds that loving the neighbour is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.' Paul calls it the fulfilment of the law, and James calls it 'the royal law' and applies it to favouritism, James 2:1-9, which is the concern of verse 15. James 5:4 echoes verse 13 on withheld wages, and Jesus' instruction to confront a brother privately, Matthew 18:15, carries forward verse 17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses meant Israel to understand that holiness is not confined to the sanctuary. The same chapter that regulates peace offerings, verses 5 to 8, also regulates harvests, wages, courts and gossip. The first hearers were to see that the God who dwelt in the tabernacle also watched the edge of the field and the scales in the market.

He meant the holiness of God to be copied, not only revered. Verse 2 does not say 'be holy because I command it,' but 'because I am holy.' Israel's life was to resemble the character of its God, and the laws of the chapter show what that resemblance looks like in practice: generosity, honesty, fairness, patience and love.

He meant the weak to be protected by the fear of God. The deaf cannot hear the curse and the blind cannot see the stumbling block, verse 14, so nobody would ever know. The law answers, 'you shall fear your God.' The same phrase returns in verse 32 for the elderly. God Himself stands guard where human accountability fails.

Finally, he meant the heart to be addressed as well as the hand. Verses 17 and 18 forbid hatred in the heart and the nursing of a grudge. Israel was to understand that the law reached inward, which is why its summary is love.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The whole chapter is prescriptive for Israel, and it is the clearest case in Leviticus of moral, ceremonial and civil law woven together. The peace offering rules of verses 5 to 8, the mixture laws of verse 19 and the fruit tree law of verses 23 to 25 belong to Israel's life at the sanctuary and in the land. The commands about parents, honesty, justice, the disabled, the elderly and the foreigner are restated throughout the New Testament and bind believers now.

The distinction is best made by following the New Testament. Jesus and the apostles repeatedly quote verses 2 and 18 and echo the laws on wages, favouritism and rebuke, while the food, fabric and planting rules are never reimposed. Some laws sit between, such as verses 27 and 28, which in context concern pagan mourning practices. Christians should apply the principle behind them, not mimicking the religious rites of unbelief, with thought and charity.

The Sabbath command of verses 3 and 30 is fulfilled in Christ's rest, Hebrews 4:9-10, though the pattern of regular rest and worship continues to shape Christian life.

debates.question: What is the point of the prohibitions on mixed breeding, mixed seed and mixed fabric in verse 19?

views.label: Living lessons in separation
views.case: Many see these laws as daily object lessons. Creation was ordered 'according to their kinds,' Genesis 1:11-12, and Israel was set apart from the nations, Leviticus 20:26. Keeping kinds distinct in field, flock and clothing reminded Israel of its own distinct calling. Notably, the tabernacle curtains and the priests' garments appear to have combined linen with dyed yarn, which many take as wool, suggesting mixture was reserved for holy things.

views.label: A guard against pagan practice
views.case: Others suggest that mixing seeds and animals had associations with the fertility practices of neighbouring peoples, so the law targeted syncretism rather than agriculture as such. The evidence for this is less direct, and the laws are presented simply as statutes, verse 19.

debates.bearing: Both views treat verse 19 as part of Israel's distinct covenant identity rather than a moral law for all people, and the New Testament does not repeat it. Deuteronomy 22:9-11 restates it with the added case of an ox and donkey yoked together, which Paul may echo in 2 Corinthians 6:14.

debates.question: Who is the 'neighbor' of verse 18?

views.label: The fellow Israelite
views.case: In its immediate context verse 18 speaks of 'any of your people,' and the parallel terms in verses 15 to 18 are 'your neighbor,' 'your people' and 'your brother.' Some Jewish interpretation in Jesus' day read it narrowly, and Jesus refers to the popular addition 'Hate your enemy,' Matthew 5:43, which is not in Leviticus.

views.label: Anyone God places in your path
views.case: The chapter itself resists a narrow reading. Verse 34 repeats the same command, 'love him as yourself,' for the resident foreigner. Jesus answers the question 'who is my neighbor?' with the parable of the Samaritan, Luke 10:29-37, turning the question around: the neighbour is the one who shows mercy, and the disciple must 'go and do likewise.'

debates.bearing: Leviticus already stretches the command beyond the family of Israel, and Jesus stretches it to its limit, including enemies, Matthew 5:44. The Christian reading follows His lead.

debates.question: Does verse 28 forbid tattoos for Christians today?

views.label: A mourning rite specific to its setting
views.case: The verse ties cuts in the body to 'the dead,' and Deuteronomy 14:1 gives the same pairing, do not cut yourselves 'on behalf of the dead.' On this view the command targets pagan mourning and religious marking, and a modern decorative tattoo is a different act.

views.label: A wider respect for the body
views.case: Others note that the tattoo clause has no explicit link to the dead and read it as a broader principle that the body belongs to God and should not be marked. They connect it to 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, 'glorify God with your body.'

debates.bearing: The verse clearly forbade Israel from marking the body in the religious ways of the nations. Beyond that, Christians should weigh motive and context with care and avoid binding the conscience where the New Testament does not.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter uses a cluster of words for the other person, and they are worth distinguishing. Verses 13, 16 and 18 use re'a, 'neighbor,' the ordinary word for a companion or fellow. Verses 11, 15 and 17 use amit, rendered 'one another' and 'neighbor,' a word for an associate or fellow member of the community. Verse 17 also uses ach, 'brother,' verse 16 speaks of 'your people,' and verse 18 of 'any of your people,' literally 'the sons of your people.' The variety shows that the chapter is thinking of the whole range of relationships in the community, and verse 34 then adds the ger, the resident foreigner, to the list.

Verse 16 contains a vivid idiom. 'You must not endanger the life of your neighbor' is, as the BSB footnote says, literally 'you must not stand against the blood of your neighbor.' It may mean standing by while a neighbour's life is threatened, or taking a stand in court that puts his life in danger. Either way, the phrase follows the command against slander, suggesting that careless words can put lives at risk. The word for 'slander,' rakil, is often connected with a trader who goes from place to place, a picture of one who carries gossip from house to house.

Verse 17 uses an emphatic Hebrew construction, the infinitive beside the finite verb, hokeach tokiach, rendered 'directly rebuke.' The same doubled form appears in God's warning in Genesis 2:17. The point is that honest confrontation, done openly, is the opposite of secret hatred, and the verse ends by saying that failure to rebuke means sharing in the other's guilt.

Verse 18 forbids two attitudes with two distinct verbs. Naqam is to take vengeance, and natar is to keep or guard, used here of nursing a grudge. The first is the act of revenge; the second is the stored resentment that prepares for it. Paul's 'Do not avenge yourselves,' Romans 12:19, stands in this line.

The word kamoka, 'as yourself,' closes both verse 18 and verse 34. In both verses the verb 'love' is followed by the preposition le, 'to' or 'toward,' which some readers take to emphasise love expressed in action toward the other.

Verse 23 calls the fruit of new trees 'forbidden,' which the BSB footnote explains as literally 'uncircumcised.' The fruit of the first three years is treated like an uncircumcised boy, not yet consecrated. In the fourth year it becomes hillulim, 'a praise offering,' verse 24. Finally, verse 19's 'two kinds,' kil'ayim, is a dual form, and it is the same term Deuteronomy 22:9 uses for mixed seed.

typology.type: Be holy, because I am holy, Leviticus 19:2
typology.fulfillment: Israel was called to resemble its God in ordinary life and consistently fell short. In Jesus the call is met in a human life. He is 'holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners,' Hebrews 7:26, and 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15. Peter repeats the call, 'just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do,' 1 Peter 1:15, and Hebrews says without holiness 'no one will see the Lord,' Hebrews 12:14. The escalation is that holiness is now received from Christ and worked out by His Spirit. The type falls short because the law could state the pattern but not reproduce it in a human heart.

typology.type: The gleaning field and the kinsman who provides, Leviticus 19:9-10
typology.fulfillment: The edges of the field were left so that the poor and the foreigner could eat. In Ruth the law brings a foreign widow to a man who goes beyond it, telling his workers to pull out extra stalks for her, Ruth 2:15-16, and then redeems her, Ruth 4:14. Boaz the redeemer becomes an ancestor of Jesus, Matthew 1:5. The pattern of the gracious provider who takes in the outsider reaches its height in Christ, who brings those 'far away' near, Ephesians 2:13. The type falls short because the field only fed the body for a season, while Christ gives Himself as the bread of life.

typology.type: Love the foreigner as yourself, Leviticus 19:33-34
typology.fulfillment: Israel was to love the resident foreigner because they had once been foreigners in Egypt. The gospel turns this into a description of every believer: Gentiles were 'strangers to the covenants of the promise,' but in Christ are 'no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints,' Ephesians 2:12 and 2:19. Christ Himself identifies with the stranger, 'I was a stranger and you took Me in,' Matthew 25:35. The escalation is that the outsider does not merely receive kindness but becomes family. The type falls short because the foreigner in Israel remained a resident alien, while in Christ there is 'neither Jew nor Greek,' Galatians 3:28.

typology.type: The ram of the guilt offering, Leviticus 19:21-22
typology.fulfillment: Even a wrong done within the limits of a harsh social order needed a guilt offering, the asham, so that the man 'will be forgiven the sin he has committed.' Isaiah 53:10 uses the same word of the Servant: 'when His soul is made a guilt offering.' Christ is the guilt offering that makes reparation for wrongs done to God and neighbour. The escalation is that the Servant gives His own life rather than a ram from the flock. The type falls short because the ram atoned for one specific wrong, while Christ's offering covers all who trust Him.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through Jesus' own use of it. When asked for the greatest commandment, He joins Deuteronomy 6:5 to Leviticus 19:18 and says, 'All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments,' Matthew 22:40. He did not invent the love command; He drew it out of this chapter and set it at the centre of the whole law. In Mark's account the scribe agrees that to love the neighbour is 'more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices,' Mark 12:33, and Jesus tells him he is 'not far from the kingdom of God,' Mark 12:34.

It leads to Christ through His interpretation. In the Sermon on the Mount He rejects the popular addition 'Hate your enemy,' Matthew 5:43, and commands love of enemies so that His disciples may be like their Father, who sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous, Matthew 5:44-45. That is Leviticus 19:2 and 19:18 read together: be like God, and God loves His enemies. When the expert in the law asks 'who is my neighbor?', Jesus tells of a Samaritan who shows mercy, Luke 10:29-37, pressing the chapter's own concern for the foreigner, verse 34.

It leads to Christ through His life. He fulfilled the command to love in a way that redefined it: 'As I have loved you, so you also must love one another,' John 13:34. His love reached those who hated Him. 'While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. When abused He 'did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23, the very spirit of verse 18, and He prayed for those who crucified Him, Luke 23:34.

It leads to Christ through the Spirit. Paul says 'the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: Love your neighbor as yourself,' Galatians 5:14, and in the same chapter he describes that love as the fruit of the Spirit. The law of Leviticus 19 is written on the heart by the one who first obeyed it.

The details of the chapter should not be pressed into pictures of Christ, as though the unripe fruit or the mixed fabric were coded prophecies. The chapter points to Him as the one who embodies its holiness and love and who gives His people the power to begin living it.
study.god:
The chapter's first word about God is that His holiness is meant to be reflected. 'Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy,' verse 2. Holiness is not only God's separation from what is common; it is a character, and the rest of the chapter shows what that character looks like: generous to the poor, fair in judgment, honest in trade, patient with offenders, loving toward strangers. To read the chapter is to see a portrait of God drawn through the laws He gives.

It shows that God watches what no one else sees. The deaf will never hear the curse, the blind will never see who placed the stumbling block, verse 14, and the elderly may be ignored without consequence, verse 32. In each case the law answers, 'you shall fear your God.' God is the witness and guardian of those who cannot defend themselves, the one who 'protects foreigners' and 'sustains the fatherless and the widow,' Psalm 146:9.

It shows that God's justice is impartial. Verse 15 forbids partiality to the poor as well as favouritism to the rich. God's concern for the vulnerable never becomes a bias that twists the truth. His justice is not a tool for any class.

It shows that God cares about the heart. The chapter moves from theft to hatred, from fraud to grudges, verses 11 to 18. God's law is not satisfied with outward compliance; it seeks love from within. This is why the chapter can be summed up in a single command.

It shows that God's redemption shapes ethics. 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,' verse 36, is attached to the command about honest weights. Israel's memory of being foreigners is the reason for loving foreigners, verse 34, and Deuteronomy 10:18 adds that God Himself 'loves the foreigner.' Grace received becomes grace extended.

For worship, the chapter refuses to separate the sanctuary from the marketplace. The same God who receives the peace offering, verse 5, weighs the merchant's scales, verse 36. True worship is a life that honours Him in every sphere, and 1 John 4:20 draws the conclusion: no one can love God whom he has not seen while hating the brother he has seen.

crossReferences.note: The call to be holy because God is holy first appears in the food laws. Leviticus 19:2 lifts it out of the kitchen and applies it to every sphere of life, showing that the same holiness governs what Israel ate and how it treated its neighbours.

The Ten Commandments echo throughout Leviticus 19: parents and Sabbath, idols, theft, false oaths, and respect for life. The chapter applies the Decalogue to farms, markets and courts, showing how its principles work out in daily detail.

Deuteronomy repeats the wage law of Leviticus 19:13 and gives its reason: the hired hand is poor and depends on his daily pay, and if it is withheld he may cry out to the LORD. Delay in paying is treated as a real injustice, not a mere inconvenience.

Moses says God executes justice for the fatherless and widow and loves the foreigner, so Israel must love the foreigner too. This grounds the command of Leviticus 19:34 not only in Israel's history but in God's own heart.

Boaz goes beyond the gleaning law of Leviticus 19:9-10, telling his workers to pull stalks from the bundles for Ruth and not to rebuke her. The law set a minimum of generosity; godly love goes further, and here it opens the door to redemption.

Amos condemns merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end so they can reduce the ephah, increase the shekel and cheat with dishonest scales. It is a direct breach of Leviticus 19:35-36, and it joins false weights to contempt for the Sabbath of verse 30.

Jesus quotes 'Love your neighbor' and rejects the addition 'Hate your enemy,' which is not in Leviticus. He calls His disciples to love enemies and to be perfect as their Father is perfect, which is the pattern of Leviticus 19:2 applied to love.

The expert in the law quotes Leviticus 19:18 and asks who his neighbour is. Jesus' parable of the Samaritan turns the question from whom I must love to whether I will be a neighbour, echoing the chapter's own extension of love to the foreigner in verse 34.

Paul says the entire law is fulfilled in the single decree of Leviticus 19:18. He sets it against the freedom that becomes an excuse for the flesh, and in the verses that follow he names love as the first fruit of the Spirit.

James forbids favouritism toward the rich and calls Leviticus 19:18 the royal law. Showing partiality breaks it, which is the concern of Leviticus 19:15. James applies the chapter directly to how a church welcomes visitors.

James warns that the withheld wages of the harvesters cry out and have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. It is Leviticus 19:13 applied to wealthy landowners of the first century, and a reminder that God hears when the powerful cheat workers.

Peter calls believers not to conform to their former passions but to be holy in all they do, quoting the Levitical call. What was addressed to Israel at Sinai is now addressed to a scattered church of Jews and Gentiles, as obedient children of a holy Father.

Paul describes Gentiles as once strangers and foreigners, far from the covenants, but now brought near by Christ's blood and made fellow citizens. The foreigner whom Leviticus 19:34 commanded Israel to love is shown to be the church itself.

study.oneStory:
At creation humanity was made in the image of God, Genesis 1:27, to reflect His character in the world. The fall broke that likeness. Cain's first question, 'Am I my brother's keeper?', Genesis 4:9, is the opposite of love of neighbour. Leviticus 19 answers both losses. It restores the call to resemble God, 'Be holy because I am holy,' and it spells out what it means to be a keeper of one's brother, sister, labourer and stranger.

The chapter also answers the exodus. God rescued a people of foreigners and slaves from Egypt, and He now shapes them into a people who will not treat others as they were treated. The memory of Egypt becomes the motive for justice, verses 34 and 36.

It sets up much of the rest of Israel's story. The prophets measure Israel against this chapter and find false scales, unpaid wages, oppressed foreigners and despised parents, Amos 8:5, Jeremiah 22:13 and Ezekiel 22:7. The call to be holy was clear, but a people with uncircumcised hearts could not answer it, and Israel went into exile.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, the true image of God, who lived the holiness of this chapter and summed it up in the love command. He died for enemies, gathered foreigners into God's household, and sent His Spirit so that the love Leviticus commanded could be produced in His people, Galatians 5:14. The gleaning field of Ruth becomes a doorway through which a foreign widow enters the line of the Messiah.

The new creation completes what this chapter began. John sees a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue' before the throne, Revelation 7:9, the foreigner fully at home. There will be no more oppression, no false measure and no withheld wage, for God will wipe every tear from His people's eyes, Revelation 21:4. The holiness Leviticus 19 described will then be the ordinary life of a whole redeemed humanity.

questions: God grounds nearly every command in this chapter with, I am the LORD. Where in your daily life, work, money, speech, do you compartmentalize away from God's character rather than letting it shape you there too?

The gleaning law built generosity to the poor directly into the structure of ordinary farming. What would it look like for you to build similar, structural generosity into your own income or schedule, rather than leaving it to occasional impulse?
Verse 18 moves from forbidding revenge and grudges straight to commanding love. Is there someone you are holding a grudge against right now whom this verse calls you to actively love instead?
Jesus names love of neighbor the second great commandment. Who is the neighbor it is hardest for you to love as yourself right now, and what would obedience look like this week?
Israel was told to love the foreigner because they themselves had been foreigners in Egypt. What past experience of your own could God be using to grow your compassion for someone different from you?

translationNotes.note: Place a stumbling block before the blind is likely both a literal command and, by extension, a principle against deliberately exploiting anyone's particular vulnerability or disadvantage.

Neighbor translates a Hebrew word, rea, whose scope this very chapter widens: verse 34 explicitly extends the same command, and the same word love, to the resident foreigner, anticipating the broader neighbor love Jesus later teaches in the parable of the Good Samaritan.

The prohibition on cutting the hair at the sides of the head and the edges of the beard likely targeted specific pagan mourning or cultic customs of the surrounding nations, rather than establishing a universal, timeless grooming law.
